newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia moves to stem tax evasion, boost revenue.
newsitem.headline: Colombia moves to stem tax evasion, boost revenue.

text.p: Colombian Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo outlined a series of measures on Tuesday intended to plug tax loopholes and clamp a 16 percent sales tax on a wide variety of services provided from abroad.

The measures, the latest announced in the country's week-old state of economic emergency, include an end to tax breaks for businesses importing raw materials and unfinished goods from outside the Andean region. Subsidiaries of foreign companies operating in Colombia will also see an end to tax benefits or exemptions on repatriated capital.
Ocampo, at a news conference, did not detail all aspects of the measures, but said they were intended to shore up tax revenues and combat tax evasion estimated at $2 billion a year.
Under the terms of a decree issued on Tuesday, no tax payer will be allowed deductions equaling more than 60 percent of their overall tax bill.
"We think that if we combat tax evasion that will go a long way to solving our problems and make up the tax shortfall (of about $800 million per year)," Ocampo said.
He said this would help narrow the government's yawning fiscal deficit that hit four percent of gross domestic product in 1996.
Other emergency measures announced last week seek to broaden the tax base, slash public spending and stem foreign debt.

Among the services that will be hit by the 16 percent sales tax are insurance and reinsurance, the protection of intellectual property rights, consultancy and entertainment offered in Colombia by foreign-based companies.

Businesses will no longer be allowed to apply for tax exemption on the value of imported raw materials and unfinished goods produced outside the Andean region but used in manufacturing processes in Colombia.
No immediate assessment was available on how much the new measures will cost businesses.

Business leaders have widely criticized elements of the overall economic emergency package as a setback to economic opening that Colombia embarked on in 1990. Many also fear the measures could exacerbate inflation, which was 21.63 percent last year -- ahead of government forecasts.

"These measures once again show we're ready to correct the problems facing us. We hope with these measures, the situation returns to normal and that we can map out a way back to more vigorous growth," Ocampo said.
